papers.title: Regulation and roles of mammalian mitophagy.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how mammalian cells selectively degrade damaged or unnecessary mitochondria through a process called mitophagy. It covers the molecular machinery involved, including receptor proteins and signaling pathways like PINK1/Parkin, that mark mitochondria for autophagic clearance. The review also discusses how mitophagy contributes to cellular health, tissue homeostasis, and disease when dysregulated, particularly in high-energy-demand tissues like the brain.
papers.why: Understanding the core molecular regulation of mitophagy is foundational to interpreting how mitochondrial quality control fails or adapts in neurons and interneurons, which is central to this PhD project's mechanistic framework.

papers.title: Dentate gyrus immaturity and region-specific synaptic and autophagy alterations across hippocampal subfields in schizophrenia.
papers.summary: This study examines the hippocampus in schizophrenia, focusing on the dentate gyrus and finding signs of cellular immaturity in its granule cells. The researchers also identify region-specific changes in synaptic proteins and autophagy markers across different hippocampal subfields. These findings suggest that disrupted neuronal maturation and altered autophagy processes may contribute to hippocampal dysfunction in schizophrenia.
papers.why: The paper's focus on region-specific autophagy alterations in hippocampal subfields directly relates to the PhD project's core interest in mitophagy/autophagy in neurons and could inform comparative analyses of interneuron and synaptic pathology across brain regions.

papers.title: Early-life exposure to polypropylene microplastics and DEHP induces ASD-relevant neurodevelopmental alterations involving mTOR-regulated autophagy impairment.
papers.summary: This study looks at how early-life exposure to polypropylene microplastics and the plasticizer DEHP affects brain development in a way that resembles autism spectrum disorder (ASD) features. The researchers found that these exposures disrupt the mTOR signaling pathway, which controls autophagy, a cellular cleanup process. This disruption in autophagy appears to underlie some of the neurodevelopmental changes observed after exposure.
papers.why: This paper connects environmental toxicant exposure to mTOR-regulated autophagy impairment in neurodevelopment, offering a disease-relevant model that could inform how autophagy/mitophagy dysregulation shapes neuronal and interneuron vulnerability in the developing brain.

papers.title: Mitochondrial complex I and II inhibiting pesticides activate DELE1-HRI integrated stress signaling but engage distinct cell death programs in human neuronal cells.
papers.summary: This paper looks at how pesticides that block mitochondrial complex I or complex II affect human neuronal cells. Both types of pesticides trigger a shared stress response pathway involving proteins called DELE1 and HRI, which normally sense mitochondrial dysfunction and alert the cell. However, despite activating this same alarm system, the two classes of pesticides ultimately push the neurons toward different mechanisms of cell death.
papers.why: Understanding how mitochondrial dysfunction and integrated stress signaling drive distinct neuronal cell death pathways is directly relevant to studying mitophagy and mitochondrial quality control in neurons, particularly for interpreting stress and damage signatures that may later be mapped spatially via transcriptomics or metabolomics.

papers.title: Screening of Stereochemically Defined 2,5-Diketopiperazines Identifies Autophagy Inducers without mTORC1 Suppression
papers.summary: This study screened a library of stereochemically defined 2,5-diketopiperazine compounds to find molecules that induce autophagy in cells. The researchers identified specific stereoisomers that activate autophagic pathways without inhibiting mTORC1 signaling, a mechanism distinct from most known autophagy inducers like rapamycin. This suggests a new class of small molecules could selectively promote autophagy while sparing mTORC1-dependent cellular processes such as growth and metabolism.
papers.why: Identifying mTORC1-independent autophagy inducers could provide novel pharmacological tools to selectively boost autophagy/mitophagy in neurons without disrupting mTORC1-dependent synaptic and metabolic functions relevant to interneuron health and perineuronal net maintenance.

papers.title: PRMT6 drives hearing loss by promoting asymmetric arginine dimethylation-mediated FOXG1 degradation and suppressing mitophagy.
papers.summary: This study finds that an enzyme called PRMT6 chemically modifies (methylates) the protein FOXG1, marking it for degradation. Loss of FOXG1 in turn suppresses mitophagy, the process that clears damaged mitochondria from cells. This chain of events contributes to hearing loss, likely by allowing damaged mitochondria to accumulate in auditory cells.
papers.why: Although focused on the ear rather than the brain, this paper offers a mechanistic model of PRMT6-mediated suppression of mitophagy via targeted protein degradation that could inform hypotheses about analogous mitophagy regulation pathways in neurons.

papers.title: Autophagy at the Crossroads of Protein and RNA Toxicity in Repeat Expansion Cerebellar Ataxias.
papers.summary: This paper discusses how autophagy, the cell's mechanism for clearing damaged components, plays a central role in repeat expansion cerebellar ataxias, a group of neurodegenerative diseases caused by abnormal DNA repeat sequences. These repeats produce both toxic proteins and toxic RNA molecules that can overwhelm or impair normal autophagy function. The paper likely reviews how disrupted autophagy contributes to neuronal damage and explores it as a potential therapeutic target in these disorders.
papers.why: Since the PhD project centers on mitophagy and autophagy dysfunction in neurons, understanding how autophagy pathways are disrupted by toxic protein and RNA species in cerebellar ataxias offers valuable mechanistic parallels relevant to neuronal degeneration research.

papers.title: Erjingwan Alleviates Parkinson's Disease via Activation of PPARA-Mediated Autophagy.
papers.summary: This paper studies Erjingwan, a traditional Chinese medicine formula, and its effects on Parkinson's Disease in an experimental model. The researchers found that it works by activating PPARA, a protein that regulates autophagy (the cell's waste-clearing process). This activation appears to protect neurons and reduce disease symptoms, suggesting a potential therapeutic mechanism.
papers.why: This paper is tangentially relevant as it explores PPARA-mediated autophagy in a neurodegenerative disease context, offering a molecular pathway that could inform mitophagy/autophagy mechanisms in neurons, though it lacks direct connections to spatial transcriptomics, interneurons, or perineuronal nets central to the profile.
